title: The Industrial Revolution Begins and Spreads
subject: AP World History

chunks.text: The Industrial Revolution was the transformation, beginning in Britain around 1750–1800, in which humans harnessed coal-fired steam power and machines to break the age-old limit on production set by human and animal muscle, wind, and water.

For all of human history before about 1800, productive power was limited by muscle, supplemented only by wind and falling water. Every society, from Rome to Song China to the Mughals, faced this muscle-shaped ceiling, which had barely moved in thousands of years.

The Industrial Revolution began in Britain because of a combination of factors, not a single cause: abundant coal and iron, capital from trade and colonies, agricultural improvements that freed up labor, and imperial access to raw materials and markets.

Britain sat on abundant, accessible deposits of coal (the fuel) and iron (the building material), often near each other and near water transport, giving it the physical resources to power and build industrial machinery.

Britain had grown wealthy from overseas trade, colonies, and the Atlantic slave-and-plantation economy, generating capital available for investment, along with banks, stable property rights, and a commerce-friendly culture.

A British Agricultural Revolution (new crops, techniques, and the enclosure of common lands) raised food output and pushed many rural people off the land, creating a large pool of available labor that could move into factories.
Britain's empire provided both raw materials, above all cotton grown by enslaved people in its colonies and the American South, and captive markets to sell finished goods, fueling industrial growth.

The Industrial Revolution began in the textile (cloth-making) industry. Inventions like the spinning jenny and the water frame mechanized spinning and weaving, multiplying output and making cotton textiles the first great industrial product.

The industrial demand for raw cotton massively intensified slavery in the American South, tying British factories directly to the expansion of plantation bondage. Industrialization and slavery grew together in this period.

The steam engine, improved decisively by James Watt in the 1760s–1780s, burned coal to boil water and used steam pressure to drive machinery. For the first time humans had a powerful, reliable energy source not dependent on muscle, wind, or a flowing river.

Because the steam engine did not depend on waterpower, a factory no longer had to be built beside a fast stream. It could be built anywhere coal could be delivered, freeing industry to concentrate in cities near labor, coal, and ports.

The Industrial Revolution involved a fundamental shift in energy: from the limited organic energy of muscle, wood, wind, and water to the concentrated, abundant fossil-fuel energy of coal. This tapped the stored energy of ancient deposits, far exceeding living muscle.

The factory system concentrated many workers operating powered machinery under one roof, replacing the older cottage industry of handwork in homes. It enabled mass production of goods in huge quantities at low cost and imposed harsh new work discipline set by the clock and the machine.

Steam power was put on wheels as the railroad locomotive and into ships as the steamship, revolutionizing transport. Goods, people, and information moved faster and more cheaply than ever before, linking factories to raw materials and global markets.

Over the 1800s industrialization spread from Britain to Western Europe (Belgium, France, the German states), the United States, and beyond. Industrialized nations grew far richer and more militarily powerful, pressuring other states to industrialize or fall behind.

Later industrializers, racing to catch up, often relied on their governments to drive industrialization from the top down, funding railroads and factories, importing experts and machines, and protecting infant industries, rather than relying on private enterprise as Britain had.

In Japan, the Meiji Restoration from 1868 saw the government deliberately and rapidly industrialize the country to avoid Western domination, building modern industries, railroads, and a modern military, and transforming Japan into a major industrial and imperial power within decades.

Russia industrialized substantially through state-directed efforts late in the 1800s, notably building the Trans-Siberian Railway. The Ottoman Empire and Qing China attempted state-led 'self-strengthening' reforms with far more limited success.

By 1900 the world had divided into industrialized 'haves' (Western Europe, North America, Japan) and non-industrialized 'have-nots.' This 'Great Divergence' in wealth and power allowed industrial states to dominate, colonize, and exploit much of the rest of the world.

The Industrial Revolution is the hinge on which global power swung: societies that could not conquer Asia's land empires in 1700 dominated most of the planet by 1900, not from greater wisdom but because they had coal-fired machines, repeating firearms, and steam warships and the others did not yet.
